scenario: You prepared for weeks for a talent show, but on the day the sound system breaks and ruins your act through no fault of your own.

choices.D: Accept the world owes you nothing, and perform anyway.
choices.A: Storm off the stage and refuse to finish your act.
choices.B: Blame yourself harshly for something that wasn't your fault.
choices.C: Insist the show gives you a special second try later.

explanation: An Absurdist embraces a world that will not always make sense, and keeps going regardless.

scenario: It rains on the one day of the year your school holds its outdoor sports day.

choices.A: Laugh at the bad luck, and enjoy the backup plan instead.
choices.B: Complain for the rest of the week that luck is against you.
choices.C: Refuse to take part once the event is rescheduled.
choices.D: Insist the whole event should be cancelled permanently.

explanation: Absurdism accepts that events won't always go as planned, and responds with good humour rather than resentment.

scenario: You spent hours on an art project for the school display, and a hallway accident smudges it right before judging.

choices.B: Accept the bad luck, and still present your work with pride.
choices.A: Hide for the rest of the day to avoid anyone seeing it.
choices.C: Blame the judges in advance for a decision they haven't made.
choices.D: Decide art was never worth doing in the first place.

explanation: The Absurdist response is to keep engaging with life and meaning-making, even when chance ruins the outcome.

scenario: Your carefully prepared group presentation slides won't open on the classroom computer.

choices.C: Laugh it off, improvise from memory, and keep presenting anyway.
choices.A: Panic and tell the teacher the group can't present at all.
choices.B: Blame one teammate for using the wrong file format.
choices.D: Refuse to speak until the slides are somehow fixed.

explanation: Absurdism responds to a senseless setback by continuing anyway, rather than letting it stop you completely.

scenario: You trained all season for a race, and it's cancelled on the morning of the event due to a random venue problem.

choices.A: Accept things don't always make sense, and try again soon.
choices.B: Decide training was pointless and quit the sport completely.
choices.C: Demand the school repay you for the wasted season.
choices.D: Stay angry about it instead of training any further.

explanation: An Absurdist keeps finding ways to act meaningfully, even when circumstances make no sense.

scenario: You accidentally studied the wrong chapter, and you still have to take today's test regardless.

choices.D: Accept the mix-up, and do your best with what you know.
choices.A: Give up on the test completely before it even starts.
choices.B: Spend the test complaining to the teacher instead of answering.
choices.C: Copy from a neighbour instead of trying with what you know.

explanation: Rather than freezing at an unfair situation, the Absurdist response is to keep going and do what you can.

scenario: You left extra early to be exactly on time, and the lift breaks down, making you late anyway.

choices.B: Shrug off the bad luck, and walk in calmly regardless.
choices.A: Arrive stressed and snap at the first person you see.
choices.C: Decide punctuality is pointless and stop trying to be on time.
choices.D: Retell the story to everyone for the rest of the day, upset.

explanation: Absurdism accepts that careful planning can still be undone by chance, and responds with calm persistence, not despair.

scenario: A joke meme mocking a school project you were proud of spreads around for no clear reason.

choices.A: Find some humour in the randomness, rather than take it seriously.
choices.B: Assume the meme proves that your work was actually bad.
choices.C: Try to track down and argue with everyone who shared it.
choices.D: Delete all your work and avoid sharing any projects again.

explanation: Absurdism recognises that reactions like this are often random and senseless, not a fair verdict on your work.

scenario: You followed every safety rule on a school hike, and still got a minor scrape from a random gust of wind.

choices.C: Accept rules don't guarantee safety, and keep hiking sensibly anyway.
choices.A: Decide following rules is pointless since it didn't guarantee safety.
choices.B: Blame the hike organisers for the unpredictable weather that day.
choices.D: Refuse to go on any future school hikes at all.

explanation: Absurdism accepts that even careful, sensible choices can't guarantee a fair or smooth result every time.

scenario: After years of perfect attendance, you catch a cold right before the ceremony that was going to recognise it.

choices.D: Accept the irony without resentment, and stay proud of what you achieved.
choices.A: Feel bitter and resentful about the timing for a long while.
choices.B: Insist on attending sick just to be seen at the ceremony.
choices.C: Decide the years of effort no longer count for anything.

explanation: The Absurdist response accepts life's ironic timing while still valuing what was genuinely achieved.

scenario: You can join the football team your parents want you to join, or the art club you truly enjoy.

choices.A: Choose based on what you value, and own the outcome.
choices.B: Join the football team quietly and never mention how you feel.
choices.C: Ask a friend to make the decision for you instead.
choices.D: Join whichever club is easiest to get into right now.

explanation: Existentialism holds that no one is born with a fixed purpose; you become responsible for the meaning you choose.

scenario: Everyone in your friend group is signing up for the same elective, and you're not sure if you actually want it too.

choices.C: Decide based on what you actually want, even if friends differ.
choices.A: Sign up automatically since that's what everyone else is doing.
choices.B: Avoid signing up for anything so you don't have to choose.
choices.D: Ask your friends to just tell you what to pick.

explanation: An authentic choice comes from your own values, not simply from copying the people around you.

scenario: You have a free Saturday with no homework and no plans.

choices.B: Choose an activity that feels genuinely meaningful or enjoyable to you.
choices.A: Do nothing all day since there's no reason to do anything.
choices.C: Wait for someone else to suggest something so you avoid deciding.
choices.D: Spend the day worrying about how to spend the day.

explanation: Existentialism says meaning isn't handed to you; you create it through the choices you actively make.

scenario: Your parents have already planned out your entire future career path for you.

choices.D: Talk honestly with them, while owning that the path is yours.
choices.A: Go along with it quietly, even though it isn't your own life.
choices.B: Refuse to discuss the topic with them at all.
choices.C: Agree out loud, but secretly ignore the plan without telling them.

explanation: Existentialism emphasises taking responsibility for your own choices, which starts with honest ownership of the decision.

scenario: A teacher says there is only one “correct” way to interpret a poem the class is studying.

choices.A: Offer your own honest interpretation, and explain your reasoning clearly.
choices.B: Repeat the teacher's interpretation without really thinking it through.
choices.C: Stay silent even though you read the poem differently.
choices.D: Say the poem is meaningless so you avoid interpreting it.

explanation: Existentialism values forming and owning your own authentic view, rather than simply adopting someone else's.

scenario: You're the only student in your class who hasn't joined any after-school club.

choices.C: Decide whether a club is meaningful to you, not just others.
choices.A: Join a random club immediately just to match everyone else.
choices.B: Feel guilty about it, but keep doing nothing anyway.
choices.D: Convince a friend to quit their club too, so you're not alone.

explanation: An authentic choice is based on what you genuinely value, not on matching what everyone else is doing.

scenario: You must pick one book for a report from a long list; none of them are required to be popular choices.

choices.B: Choose the book that genuinely interests you, and stand by it.
choices.A: Pick whichever book your friends picked, even if it doesn't interest you.
choices.C: Pick the shortest book without thinking about whether you'll enjoy it.
choices.D: Ask the teacher to just assign you one book.

explanation: Existentialism encourages choosing based on genuine interest and standing behind that choice.

scenario: A friend pressures you to copy their opinion during a class debate instead of forming your own.

choices.A: Form and state your own honest position on the topic.
choices.B: Copy their opinion exactly, since it's easier than thinking it through.
choices.C: Stay completely silent for the debate to avoid any disagreement.
choices.D: Agree with your friend out loud, then complain about it privately.

explanation: Existentialism holds you responsible for your own genuine views, rather than borrowing someone else's to avoid discomfort.

scenario: You're unsure what you want to do after secondary school, and it feels like there's no single “right answer” already written for you.

choices.D: Treat the uncertainty as freedom to shape your own path.
choices.A: Panic, since you feel there must be one correct path somewhere.
choices.B: Let your parents decide everything so you don't have to think.
choices.C: Avoid thinking about the future until it's forced on you.

explanation: Existentialism reframes the lack of a fixed, ready-made purpose as freedom and responsibility, not as a flaw to fix.

scenario: Your team loses a group award because you insisted on doing your part your own way instead of following the group's original plan.

choices.C: Accept responsibility for the outcome, and reflect honestly.
choices.A: Blame the group for not appreciating your different approach.
choices.B: Pretend the outcome wasn't really caused by your decision.
choices.D: Decide you'll never make your own decisions in a group again.

explanation: Existentialism requires owning the consequences of your freely chosen actions, including honest reflection afterward.

scenario: You have one hour before a test tomorrow: you can play your favourite game now, or review your notes.

choices.D: Review your notes now, and play the game afterward instead.
choices.A: Play the game the whole hour, since it feels better right now.
choices.B: Do neither, and spend the hour worrying instead.
choices.C: Study so intensely that you skip sleep entirely tonight.

explanation: Enlightened Hedonism weighs short-term fun against the longer-term pain of a bad result, and chooses the better overall balance.

scenario: You can eat your favourite candy right before dinner, or wait until afterward.

choices.C: Wait until after dinner, avoiding a spoiled appetite and discomfort.
choices.A: Eat it right away since it's more satisfying in the moment.
choices.B: Refuse to ever eat candy, even on special occasions.
choices.D: Eat double the amount now to feel extra good immediately.

explanation: Waiting avoids a worse experience shortly after, making it the choice with the better overall pleasure balance.

scenario: Skipping your homework tonight to watch a show sounds fun, but the homework is due first period tomorrow.

choices.A: Do the homework first, then relax, since tomorrow's stress outweighs tonight's fun.
choices.B: Watch the show, and deal with the consequences tomorrow.
choices.C: Stay up very late trying to do both at once, exhausted.
choices.D: Skip the show, and refuse to relax at all tonight.

explanation: A wise Hedonist compares tonight's fun against tomorrow's stress, and picks the option with better overall balance.

scenario: Staying up late gaming feels great, but you have an early school trip departure tomorrow morning.

choices.B: Consider tomorrow's tiredness, and choose to sleep earlier instead.
choices.A: Stay up as late as you want, since gaming feels good now.
choices.C: Refuse to game at all tonight, even for a short while.
choices.D: Stay up all night, and skip the trip instead.

explanation: Sleeping earlier trades a bit of tonight's fun for a much better, well-rested experience tomorrow — a better overall balance.

scenario: A classmate offers to let you copy their answers on tonight's homework, which feels like an easy relief right now.

choices.C: Do the work yourself, since relief now isn't worth later confusion.
choices.A: Copy the answers immediately for the quick relief.
choices.B: Report the classmate to the teacher without talking to them first.
choices.D: Copy only some answers, thinking it's a fair compromise.

explanation: A wise Hedonist looks past the immediate ease toward the bigger, longer-term discomfort it could cause later.

scenario: You can spend all your allowance on snacks today, or save some for a trip you're excited about next month.

choices.D: Save some of it now, for more enjoyment on next month's trip.
choices.A: Spend it all today since that feels good right now.
choices.B: Save all of it, and buy nothing enjoyable today either.
choices.C: Spend it all today, and borrow money later to make up for it.

explanation: Balancing some enjoyment now with saving for later usually produces more overall pleasure than spending everything immediately.

scenario: Practising a difficult piano piece is boring right now, but skipping practice means struggling more at the recital.

choices.A: Accept some boredom now, for less recital stress later.
choices.B: Skip practice today, since it isn't fun right now.
choices.C: Practise for so long it becomes exhausting and no longer enjoyable.
choices.D: Quit piano completely, since practice isn't always fun to do.

explanation: A wise Hedonist accepts a little short-term discomfort when it clearly leads to greater pleasure and less pain later.

scenario: You're tempted to prank a friend for a quick laugh, even though it might upset them for the rest of the day.

choices.C: Weigh your brief laugh against their longer discomfort before deciding.
choices.A: Do the prank anyway, since your own amusement matters most.
choices.B: Prank them, but blame someone else if they end up upset.
choices.D: Avoid your friend all day to dodge any reaction.

explanation: Hedonism, done wisely, considers the total pleasure and pain involved for everyone affected, not just your own quick laugh.

scenario: Watching videos feels more appealing than going outside to play sports with friends today.

choices.B: Consider which one actually leaves you feeling better afterward.
choices.A: Watch videos all day, since it feels easiest right now.
choices.C: Force yourself outside even while genuinely unwell, ignoring how you feel.
choices.D: Avoid deciding, and end up doing neither activity.

explanation: A wise Hedonist checks which choice leads to better overall enjoyment afterward, not only which feels easiest in the moment.

scenario: You could rush through a chores task to go play sooner, but rushing usually means redoing it properly later.

choices.D: Do it properly the first time, avoiding a bigger hassle later.
choices.A: Rush through it badly so you can go play immediately.
choices.B: Refuse to do the chore at all so you can play now.
choices.C: Do it so slowly that you have no time left to play.

explanation: Doing it properly the first time avoids a bigger, less enjoyable hassle later — a better overall balance of effort and reward.

scenario: You spent all afternoon building a sandcastle. The tide washes it away before anyone else sees it. “It didn't matter, since nothing lasts” — how would you respond to this idea?

choices.C: The joy was in building it, so it mattered regardless.
choices.A: Agree completely, and stop building anything ever again.
choices.B: Get angry at the tide for taking something that mattered.
choices.D: Refuse to think about the question at all.

explanation: This reframes Nihilism's challenge with an Absurdist/Existentialist-style answer: value can come from the experience itself, not only from permanence.

scenario: You practised piano for weeks for a recital that got cancelled and never rescheduled. “Was practising pointless since no one ever heard it?”

choices.B: The skill and enjoyment from practising are still real.
choices.A: Yes, decide there's no point practising anything without an audience.
choices.C: Blame the people who cancelled the recital for wasting your time.
choices.D: Avoid answering the question and change the subject.

explanation: The value of practice doesn't only come from being witnessed; the growth and enjoyment are real either way.

scenario: A card tower you built falls over the moment you finish it. “If it doesn't last, why bother building it?”

choices.A: The fun and focus while building still counted.
choices.B: Agree, and stop building anything that won't last forever.
choices.C: Get angry and refuse to build anything else today.
choices.D: Insist the question doesn't matter, and ignore it.

explanation: Enjoyment and focus during an activity are real value, even when the result itself is temporary.

scenario: You help an elderly neighbour carry groceries, and they forget your name by next week. “Does a kind act matter if it isn't remembered?”

choices.D: The help still mattered in that moment, whether or not it's remembered.
choices.A: No, decide it's not worth helping people who won't remember you.
choices.B: Feel resentful that your kindness wasn't recognised properly.
choices.C: Avoid the question by pretending you never think about it.

explanation: An act's value can exist in the moment it happens, independent of whether it's remembered afterward.

scenario: Your class picks up litter at the beach, but new litter appears again the very next day. “Was the clean-up pointless since it didn't last?”

choices.B: The beach was safer for a while, and habits add up.
choices.A: Yes, decide clean-ups are a waste of time and stop doing them.
choices.C: Blame whoever litters instead of thinking about the question.
choices.D: Refuse to think about it further and just move on.

explanation: Temporary results can still be genuinely valuable, especially as part of a repeated, ongoing habit.

scenario: You spent a whole afternoon preparing a joke that only made one friend laugh, and they forgot it by the next day. “Was it worth the effort for one laugh nobody remembers?”

choices.C: Shared moments have value in the moment, regardless.
choices.A: No, decide jokes are pointless if nobody remembers them.
choices.B: Feel embarrassed about it, and avoid telling jokes again.
choices.D: Ignore the question completely and move on.

explanation: A moment of genuine connection or joy is meaningful when it happens, whether or not it's remembered afterward.

scenario: In a hundred years, almost no one will remember your name. “So why try hard at anything now?”

choices.A: The people and choices around you now are real.
choices.B: Agree completely, and stop putting effort into anything.
choices.C: Get anxious, and avoid thinking about the future at all.
choices.D: Decide only famous people's actions can really matter.

explanation: This answers Nihilism's challenge with an Existentialist-style point: present impact and relationships are real value now.

scenario: You train hard for a school race. Even if you win, next year almost no one will remember who won. “Does winning matter if it's forgotten?”

choices.B: The growth and pride from training belong to you regardless.
choices.A: No, decide there's no point training or competing at all.
choices.C: Only try hard when you're sure people will remember it.
choices.D: Refuse to answer, and avoid thinking about it.

explanation: Personal growth and pride from effort remain real and yours, independent of how long other people remember the result.

scenario: A sandwich you carefully made for lunch is eaten and gone within five minutes. “Was making it worth the effort, since it doesn't last?”

choices.D: Some things are meant to be enjoyed, and that's fine.
choices.A: No, decide that preparing food carefully is basically a waste.
choices.B: Feel annoyed that the sandwich didn't last a bit longer.
choices.C: Avoid thinking about the question, and change the subject fast.

explanation: Not everything needs to be permanent to be worthwhile; some value comes precisely from being enjoyed in the moment.

scenario: Your school will one day be demolished and rebuilt, so nothing about the building is permanent. “Does anything you do here actually matter?”

choices.C: Your friendships and experiences here are meaningful now, permanence aside.
choices.A: No, decide nothing at a temporary place can really matter.
choices.B: Feel discouraged, and stop caring about school entirely.
choices.D: Avoid the question, and think about something else instead.

explanation: This responds to Nihilism's challenge by locating meaning in present relationships and experience, not in permanence.

scenario: Your group-project teammate did not finish their part before the deadline, and the presentation is in 10 minutes.

choices.B: Calmly cover the missing part yourself and present your best work.
choices.A: Blame your teammate loudly in front of the whole class.
choices.C: Refuse to take part in the presentation at all.
choices.D: Complain about the unfairness instead of preparing anything.

explanation: A Stoic focuses only on their own actions, which are within their control, and accepts what is not.

scenario: You studied hard for a test, but got a lower grade than expected because the teacher changed the question format at the last minute.

choices.A: Accept the result calmly, and adjust your studying approach next time.
choices.B: Argue with the teacher that the whole test was unfair.
choices.C: Decide studying never works and stop preparing for tests.
choices.D: Stay upset about the grade for the rest of the week.

explanation: The format change was outside your control; how you respond and prepare next time is not.

scenario: It starts raining right before your outdoor birthday party is about to begin.

choices.C: Accept the weather calmly, and switch to your indoor plan.
choices.A: Blame whoever chose an outdoor venue for the party.
choices.B: Cancel the party completely and send everyone home early.
choices.D: Spend the party complaining about the rain to your guests.

explanation: The weather can't be controlled, but how calmly and quickly you adapt to it can.

scenario: Your bus is late, and you're going to miss the start of a school assembly.

choices.D: Stay calm, since worrying won't help, and plan your next step.
choices.A: Message everyone that the bus company ruined your morning.
choices.B: Get off early and sprint the rest of the way, panicking.
choices.C: Decide to skip the assembly completely out of frustration.

explanation: A Stoic doesn't waste energy on what they can't change, and instead plans their next controllable step.

scenario: You're picked last for a team during PE class.

choices.A: Accept it wasn't your choice, then play your best anyway.
choices.B: Refuse to play for the rest of the lesson.
choices.C: Tell the teacher the picking system is completely unfair.
choices.D: Sulk on the sidelines instead of joining the game properly.

explanation: Other people's choices about you are outside your control; your own effort afterward is not.

scenario: A friend cancels plans with you at the last minute for the third time this month.

choices.B: Calmly plan your time, then share how the pattern feels.
choices.A: Send an angry message demanding an explanation right now.
choices.C: Assume the friendship is over and stop replying to them.
choices.D: Pretend you don't care at all, even though you're upset.

explanation: You can't control your friend's choices, but you can control your own reaction and how you communicate.

scenario: You lose a chess tournament final after a strong season of practice.

choices.C: Focus on what you did, since training is yours.
choices.A: Decide the whole season of practice was a waste.
choices.B: Blame the organisers for giving you an unfair schedule.
choices.D: Avoid playing chess again so you can't lose again.

explanation: The outcome of a single match isn't fully within your control; your preparation and growth are.

scenario: Your phone breaks the night before an important school trip.

choices.A: Stay calm, and focus on packing what you actually need.
choices.B: Panic and stay up all night worrying about the phone.
choices.C: Blame your family for not buying a sturdier phone.
choices.D: Decide the whole trip is ruined before it even starts.

explanation: The phone breaking is done and outside your control; preparing well for the trip is still within it.

scenario: A rumour about you that isn't fully true starts spreading around school.

choices.D: Calmly correct the facts once, then let the rest go.
choices.A: Track down and confront everyone who repeated the rumour.
choices.B: Spread a rumour back at whoever started this one.
choices.C: Avoid places where you might meet people who heard it.

explanation: You can't control what everyone believes, but you can control whether you respond with calm honesty.

scenario: You're not chosen for the lead role in the school play, even though you prepared well for the audition.

choices.B: Accept the casting decision, then give full effort to your actual role.
choices.A: Quit the play since you didn't get the role you wanted.
choices.C: Tell the director their decision was a mistake and demand a recast.
choices.D: Perform half-heartedly to show everyone you're upset about it.

explanation: The casting decision was outside your control; how well you perform your actual role is not.

scenario: As class monitor, you have only 5 fun-fair tickets for a class of 30 students who all worked equally hard.

choices.D: Hold a raffle so every student has an equal chance.
choices.A: Give the tickets to your close friends first.
choices.B: Sell the tickets to whoever offers the most money.
choices.C: Keep the tickets and let students argue it out themselves.

explanation: Utilitarianism seeks the greatest good for the greatest number; a fair, transparent raffle best respects everyone's equal effort.

scenario: You're planning a class party with a fixed budget; some classmates want games, others want more food.

choices.B: Choose the mix that most classmates would enjoy.
choices.A: Spend the whole budget on whatever you personally prefer.
choices.C: Let whoever complains the loudest decide everything for the class.
choices.D: Split the budget evenly without asking anyone what they'd enjoy.

explanation: Utilitarianism looks at overall wellbeing, so gathering input and maximising total enjoyment is the better approach.

scenario: Your group of 4 has only one laptop with a battery about to die, and several small tasks left to finish.

choices.A: Use the battery on whichever task helps the group most.
choices.B: Let whoever grabs the laptop first keep it the whole time.
choices.C: Argue about who deserves the laptop most based on friendship.
choices.D: Turn the laptop off entirely so no one can use it.

explanation: Utilitarianism directs a limited resource toward the choice that benefits the group's overall progress the most.

scenario: Your class has only 20 rulers to share between 30 students during a measuring activity.

choices.C: Set up a fair rotation so more students get a turn.
choices.A: Let the first 20 students to grab one keep it all lesson.
choices.B: Give rulers only to your close friends first.
choices.D: Hide an extra ruler so you always have one to yourself.

explanation: A fair rotation gives the most students access to the limited resource, maximising overall benefit.

scenario: As team captain, you must choose which 5 of 8 equally-skilled players start a friendly match.

choices.B: Rotate players fairly so more people get meaningful playing time.
choices.A: Always start your closest friends regardless of fairness.
choices.C: Let only the loudest players decide who starts each game.
choices.D: Pick players randomly with no real plan for the season.

explanation: A fair rotation plan maximises the overall benefit (playing time and enjoyment) across the whole team over time.

scenario: Your school can fund either a new library reading corner or a new sports item, based on a student vote, but not both.

choices.D: Support whichever option most students would genuinely benefit from.
choices.A: Push for whichever option benefits you personally, regardless of the vote.
choices.B: Ignore the vote, and let a small group of friends decide privately.
choices.C: Refuse to take part in the decision at all.

explanation: Utilitarianism supports the option that creates the greatest overall benefit, which a fair vote helps identify.

scenario: You notice a small rule in a game your friends invented that happens to benefit you personally, but makes the game less fun for everyone else.

choices.A: Suggest changing the rule so the game feels fairer overall.
choices.B: Say nothing, and quietly keep benefiting from the unfair rule.
choices.C: Insist on keeping the rule since you personally benefit from it.
choices.D: Quit the game entirely rather than raise the issue.

explanation: Utilitarianism weighs the good of the whole group above one person's private advantage.

scenario: Only one prize is left for a class quiz, and there's an exact tie between two teams.

choices.B: Propose a fair tie-breaker that keeps the contest enjoyable.
choices.A: Give the prize to whichever team you personally prefer.
choices.C: Refuse to award any prize at all out of frustration.
choices.D: Let the two teams settle it however they want, unsupervised.

explanation: A fair, well-run tie-breaker maximises enjoyment and fairness for the whole class, not just the two teams involved.

scenario: Your group project can either try a flashy but risky idea that might impress the teacher, or use a safer idea that guarantees the whole group passes.

choices.C: Weigh which choice creates the best outcome for the group.
choices.A: Choose the risky idea purely because it's more exciting for you.
choices.B: Let one person decide alone without asking the rest of the group.
choices.D: Refuse to decide, and let the deadline pass without a plan.

explanation: Utilitarianism asks you to consider the consequences for everyone affected, not just personal excitement.

scenario: A charity walk lets you pick one of three routes; a slightly longer route raises more donations for the whole school's charity total.

choices.D: Choose the route that helps the most, despite the extra effort.
choices.A: Pick the shortest route since it's more comfortable for you.
choices.B: Pick a route at random without considering the impact.
choices.C: Refuse to walk at all if it isn't the easiest option.

explanation: Utilitarianism supports accepting a personal cost when it produces a clearly greater overall benefit for others.
